en: *Essential Notes on the Observance and Violation of the Bodhisattva Precepts*, composed by the Silla śramaṇa Wonhyo. Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts:
they are the great ford for returning the flow to its source, and the essential means for abandoning the heterodox to follow the orthodox.
This is the gateway. Yet,
the characteristics of the heterodox and the orthodox are easily confused,
and the natures of transgression and merit are difficult to distinguish.
Why is this? Because there may be those whose internal intentions are actually perverse, yet whose external traces appear correct;
or those whose manifest karma is defiled.
Yet their inner minds are pure.
Or there may be those whose actions, though associated with little merit,
lead to great calamity.
There are those whose mental activities accord with what is profound and remote,
yet oppose what is shallow and near;
for this reason, they are exclusively defiled practitioners of the Way.
The śramaṇa who carves out his own private interests will long remain attached to mere outward traces,
thereby losing the true and correct [path].
Every time one establishes profound precepts,
yet seeks only shallow practices;
now, I shall set aside these shallow matters.
Yet, while remaining entirely profound,
he departs from what appears to be a mere trace to pursue the reality; this is because he has,
for his own sake, suddenly forgotten [the superficial].
This is a summary of the recorded instructions.
May those who share this same aspiration examine it closely and resolve upon the essentials of what constitutes transgression and non-transgression.
There are three gates:
first, the gate of lightness and heaviness;

There are those that are common and those that are uncommon; the characteristics of the common and the uncommon can be understood from the text.

Just as one knows that in the customs and practices of the world at this time,
there are many who detest those who praise themselves and disparage others,
while they always revere those who are self-effacing and extol others.
Furthermore, one knows that if one disparages another, that person will surely revile oneself;
and if one praises another, that person will in turn commend oneself.
It is by knowing this that [one acts accordingly].
To craftily seek self-exaltation and to disparage oneself while praising others constitutes a grave offense.
If one knows that what others uphold is unreasonable,
it may be abandoned;
that which is understood within oneself is the path.
One should cultivate upright aspiration to establish the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings;
one must not praise oneself and disparage others.
This constitutes great merit.
As for the third phrase:
it is like a certain type of disposition.
They are full of deception and falsehood;
desiring to delude the people of the world,
they disparage the superior qualities of others.
Concealing one's own shortcomings,
it is for this reason that one utters evasive and confused speech.
To disparage one's own minor virtues is a fault;
to praise the shortcomings of others as one's own achievement is a fault;
to proclaim one's many faults as a virtue is a fault.
Furthermore, taking the strengths of others as faults;
moreover, there is another class who are naturally upright by disposition.
It is for the purpose of guiding the people of the world so that they may recognize good and distinguish evil,
abandon transgressions, and cultivate merit.
Because of this resolve,
one speaks directly without deviation and perceives one's own faults.
One must certainly disparage [one's own faults] and immediately praise upon hearing of the goodness of others.
Recognizing one's own virtues, one praises them;
knowing another's faults, one directly censures them.
When those who came before slandered or praised, or suppressed or exalted,
it was simply the sin of deceit and flattery;
when later scholars censured or sighed over, or lauded or disparaged [them], it was likewise so.
This is also the blessing of loyalty and uprightness.
As for the fourth phrase,
it refers to those of a noble character.
This profound and noble one lets his spirit roam within the embrace of the uncarved simplicity;
he does not know where the beginning lies,
blending together both calamity and fortune.
Returning to oneness and forgetting self and other constitutes non-duality.
Their spirits are always joyful because they roam in this place; furthermore,
they neither disparage themselves nor praise others.
Nor do they exalt themselves or disparage others.
Furthermore, there are those of inferior and foolish nature whose dispositions are dull and simple,
such that they cannot distinguish between right and wrong.
They find it difficult to distinguish between beans and barley;
they do not recognize what is good as being good,
nor do they understand what is evil as being evil.
Their minds are constantly clouded because they have forgotten both hatred and attachment; furthermore,
they neither disparage themselves nor praise others.
Furthermore, there is no self-praise or disparagement of others;
this is the fault of the dull-witted and ignorant,
while that is the blessing of the pure and simple wise.
This is called the fourfold formulation for judging demerit and merit;
it relies upon the first two lines.
Then meritorious karma transforms into a grave affliction,
while sinful karma becomes a great virtue.
This follows from the latter two lines.
Thus, his speech was free from deception;
he conversed with loyalty without reserve.
He possessed superior wisdom.
By following the same outward conduct as the ignorant and foolish,
one knows that this is the essential point for a practitioner regarding the observance and violation of precepts.
One should merely examine subtly one's own gains and losses;
one must not hastily judge the virtues or faults of others.
Such is the underlying intent regarding the depth of upholding or violating the precepts.
Third, regarding the explanation of ultimate observance and violation:
although one may rely on the dharma-gates as previously explained and be able to recognize the nature of what is light and what is heavy, [the following applies].
While they understand the characteristics of both the shallow and the profound,
they do not comprehend the aspects of the precepts as they truly are.
Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not,
one who has not yet abandoned the two extremes cannot ultimately maintain [the precepts] without transgression.
One does not proceed toward the perfection of pure ethical discipline. Why is this?
It is because ethical discipline is not self-generated.
Since it must rely on various conditions,
it certainly lacks any intrinsic characteristic;
thus, the conditions themselves are not the precepts.
Apart from conditions there is no precept; to eliminate [the conditions] is itself to eliminate [the precept].
One cannot obtain anything in between.
Seeking precepts in this manner,
they are ultimately not existent; thus, one cannot speak of them as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is not established [as a substantial entity],
it relies upon various conditions; yet,
it is not that precepts do not exist.
It is not like a rabbit's horn,
for it lacks causes and conditions;
it is as described in the characteristics of the precepts.
The characteristics of offenses are likewise;
as are the characteristics of precepts and offenses,
so too are the characteristics of persons.
If, within this context,
one relies on what is not existent and views it as being utterly non-existent, [that is a wrong view].
Although it is said that there is no transgression,
one has nonetheless permanently lost the precepts,
because one has slandered and rejected the mere phenomenal aspects of the precepts.
Furthermore, within this context,
those who reckon that something exists based on its non-non-existence [impute existence].
Although it is said that one can maintain [the precepts], such maintenance is itself a transgression,
for it violates the true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the precepts.
When a bodhisattva cultivates ethical discipline, it is not like this;
although they do not conceive of a subject who maintains or an object that is maintained.
Yet one does not disparage or deny the mere fact of the precepts; therefore,
there is ultimately no grave transgression of losing the precepts,
even if one does not perceive whether something is non-offensive or offensive.
Yet they do not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the precepts;
therefore, they are forever free from even subtle transgressions of the precepts.
This is due to such skillful means and profound wisdom.
Forever forgetting the three spheres and not falling into the two extremes,
one then proceeds toward the perfection of the full precepts.
As the sutra says:
"Transgression" and "non-transgression."
Because it is unattainable,
one should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
The root text of the precepts states:
The light of the precepts issues from the mouth;
it has its conditions and is not without cause.
Neither form, nor mind,
nor existence.
It is not non-existent;
it is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas.
This is the root of the bodhisattva.
Herein, the term "light of ethical discipline" (śīlaprabhā) is used to manifest both ethical discipline and light.
They are non-dual and undifferentiated,
for luminous purity and defilement are of one single flavor; therefore,
one contemplates the light of the precepts.
This reveals the true nature of precepts:
precepts lack intrinsic nature because they necessarily depend upon other conditions.
It is said: "There are conditions.
These words regarding conditions do not rely on [the existence of] being.
It directly reveals that it is not without its causal source;
therefore, it is said to be "not causeless.
It is not that the nature of the precept is causeless.
It is neither material obstruction nor cognitive discernment; therefore,
it is said to be neither form nor mind.
Although it is neither form nor mind,
it can never be found apart from form and mind.
Although it cannot be apprehended,
it is not that precepts do not exist;
therefore, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Although it is not that there is no precept,
it is devoid of its fruit because it lacks its cause.
Being devoid of cause and lacking effect,
it is therefore called a phenomenon that is neither cause nor effect.
Precepts serve as the causal nature;
although they cannot be apprehended,
they give rise to the fruition of all Buddhas.
It must rely on the cause of precepts;
therefore, it is said to be the fundamental source of all Buddhas.
Precepts constitute the nature of the fruit.
Although it cannot be apprehended,
the precepts necessarily rely upon the cause of the bodhicitta;
therefore, they are said to be the root of a bodhisattva.
Question: Such are the characteristics of the precepts;
they are profoundly deep and difficult to understand.
Even to comprehend them is still a challenge.
How much more so for one who practices cultivation!
Therefore, it should be known that the characteristics of practice are as previously described.
This is practiced solely by great earth bodhisattvas;
it does not concern the conduct of those who have newly resolved their minds.
[The answer] is found in the sutra.
The direct answer is as you have asked:
it is said that from the very first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment,
a bodhisattva constantly practices the dharma of non-apprehension.
Because of the dharma of non-apprehension,
one practices giving and maintains the precepts;
and so on, up to because of the dharma of non-apprehension.
"Therefore, one cultivates wisdom.
The meaning of this response is that if one were to cause those [beings] to practice...
Because it has never been practiced before and is difficult to perform,
one does not practice it now.
Because one does not practice now,
one will likewise not cultivate it later.
Thus it continues for a long time.
It is exceedingly difficult; therefore,
one is made to look up to and practice its difficulty from the very beginning,
so that through gradual cultivation, the practice increases.
Transforming what is difficult into what is easy—
this is called the great intention for embarking upon new practice.
It is the ultimate mastery of both observance and transgression.

Thus have I briefly explained this, relying upon the definitive scriptures of the sages. I have roughly described the essential gateways of the Treasury of Precepts, universally lighting a single lamp for the entire Dharma realm; may it serve to transmit the lamp throughout the ten directions.
The fourfold statements and the three clusters of precepts are perfected; through the six mental applications and five cultivations, they are brought to completion.
By remaining far removed from the two extremes, all transgressions are extinguished. Equal partaking in the single flavor, wandering beyond the mundane world.

*Hijō Yōki* (Essential Record of Transgressions and Observances), one scroll. Completed on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the second year of Kwan’en, the Year of the Wood Dragon (1324).

At the time of his travels to the Southern Capital (Nanjing) in the sixteenth year of Kōei, the monk Shin-nin of Daitō-ji Temple exhorted [the donor] to transcribe this from an ancient manuscript of the Jōshō-in of Tōdai-ji Temple; he did so with the hope that the lamp of the Vinaya might be transmitted without end.
Recorded by a minor bhikṣu while staying at Quanyong.
